terms.meaning: England's top division. Twenty clubs, each plays the other nineteen twice, August to May.
terms.heard: Constantly. It is the whole thing.
terms.sayIt: "Is that a Premier League game or one of the cups?"
terms.overheard: Premier League is back Saturday. Three months of my life, gone.
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: England's top division, twenty clubs, August to May
decoys: The league for the top clubs in Britain
All the English divisions taken together

terms.meaning: The start of the match, and the restart after half-time or a goal.
terms.heard: "What time's kick-off?" about eight times a weekend.
terms.sayIt: "What time's kick-off? I'll come and watch the start."
terms.overheard: Kick-off's at three. I'll be no use to anyone after that.
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: The moment the match starts
decoys: The coin toss that decides which way to play
The first shot that tests the keeper

terms.meaning: The fifteen-minute break in the middle. Kettle time, and the manager's chance to shout.
terms.heard: "Half-time team talk" when the manager needs to fix things.
terms.sayIt: "Half-time. What did you make of that?"
terms.overheard: Right, that's half-time. I'm putting the kettle on, do you want one?
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: The break in the middle of the match
decoys: The fifteen minutes before kick-off
A short break for drinks in hot weather

terms.meaning: The end of the match. The referee blows and it is over, whatever the score.
terms.heard: "FT" in a text. Then either celebration or silence.
terms.sayIt: "Full-time. Right, where does that leave us?"
terms.overheard: Full-time here. They'll take that, I'm sure.
terms.speaker: telly
terms.gist: The referee ends it, whatever the score
decoys: The end of the first of the two halves
The whistle that starts the added minutes

terms.meaning: The league standings, top to bottom. Top wins the title, the bottom three go down.
terms.heard: "Where are we in the table?" He knows. He wants to say it.
terms.sayIt: "Where does that leave them in the table?"
terms.overheard: Have a look at the table and tell me that's fair.
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: Every club ordered by points won
decoys: A fixture list for the weekend's games
The clubs sorted by goals scored so far

terms.meaning: When the ball is passed to you, you can't already be nearer the goal than the last defender. If you are, the flag goes up and the goal doesn't count.
terms.heard: Every time a flag goes up and someone on the sofa groans.
terms.sayIt: "Was he offside? He looked level to me."
terms.overheard: That's never offside. I don't care what the replay says.
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: He was beyond the final defender for the pass
decoys: The ball had already gone out for a goal kick
He got in the keeper's way at the near post

terms.meaning: A free shot from twelve yards with only the goalkeeper to beat. Given for a foul or handball inside the box. Scored about three times in four.
terms.heard: A gasp, then nobody speaks until it's taken.
terms.sayIt: "Penalty! Who takes them for us?"
terms.overheard: Penalty. The whole ground has gone quiet.
terms.speaker: telly
terms.gist: A free shot with just the keeper to beat
decoys: A punishment card shown after a bad tackle
A free kick given just outside the box

terms.meaning: Video Assistant Referee. Someone in a room checks goals, penalties and red cards on replay and tells the referee if he got it badly wrong.
terms.heard: "VAR is checking" followed by two minutes of silence.
terms.sayIt: "Hang on, VAR's checking it. Don't celebrate yet."
terms.overheard: VAR has been the story of this season, for better or worse.
terms.speaker: telly
terms.gist: The video referee is looking at the replay
decoys: A panel that reviews decisions after the match
The screen in the ground showing the decision

terms.meaning: A warning from the referee. Two in one game and you are sent off.
terms.heard: "He's on a yellow" means the player has to be careful now.
terms.sayIt: "He's on a yellow, he needs to calm down."
terms.overheard: yellow card for that? he's barely touched him.
terms.speaker: chat
terms.gist: A formal warning, two and you are off
decoys: A fine the club pays the league
A ban from the next match, straight away

terms.meaning: Sent off. The player leaves and the team plays the rest of the game one short. A straight red is for one bad act; two yellows also make a red.
terms.heard: "Straight red" means one bad tackle, no warning first.
terms.sayIt: "That's a red. He's off."
terms.overheard: Red card. Well, that's the game gone.
terms.speaker: pundit
terms.gist: A player off, and nobody replaces him
decoys: A warning before he is sent off
A penalty given against them for the foul

terms.meaning: Three for a win, one for a draw, none for a loss. Add them up and that is the table.
terms.heard: "Three points is three points" after any ugly win.
terms.sayIt: "Ugly, but it's three points."
terms.overheard: didnt deserve that at all but ill take the points.
terms.speaker: chat
terms.gist: Three for a win, one for a draw
decoys: One for every goal scored
A tally handed out by finishing position

terms.meaning: Goals scored minus goals let in. Two teams level on points are split by it. A 3-0 win is worth more than a 1-0 win for this reason.
terms.heard: Late in the season when two teams are neck and neck.
terms.sayIt: "Level on points, so it'll come down to goal difference."
terms.overheard: I think this one goes to goal difference. That's a worry.
terms.speaker: pundit
terms.gist: Goals scored minus goals let in
decoys: The margin in a single match
A gap in points between two clubs

terms.meaning: The bottom three at the end of the season drop down a division, to the Championship. Losing money, players and pride in one go.
terms.heard: "Relegation battle" from about February onwards.
terms.sayIt: "They're in a relegation battle, aren't they?"
terms.overheard: If we don't win tonight we're in a relegation scrap by Christmas.
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: Dropping out of the division at the bottom
decoys: A player pushed down to the reserves
Finishing outside the places for Europe

terms.meaning: Going up a division. Three clubs come up from the Championship each summer to replace the three that went down.
terms.heard: In May, usually with someone crying on a pitch.
terms.sayIt: "Who came up this year?"
terms.overheard: mate they've done it. promotion with three games to spare.
terms.speaker: chat
terms.gist: Moving up into the division above
decoys: A move up into the first team
Finishing top of the division, champions

terms.meaning: Finishing in the first four places, which earns a Champions League spot for next season. The realistic target for clubs who won't win the title.
terms.heard: "Top four is the aim" from big clubs that won't win the title.
terms.sayIt: "Top four is the aim this year, surely?"
terms.overheard: Top four, and he'd call the season a success.
terms.speaker: pundit
terms.gist: A finish high enough for Champions League
decoys: Winning the league and lifting the trophy
The sides who reach a cup semi-final

terms.meaning: The big rectangle in front of each goal, eighteen yards deep. A foul in there is a penalty. Also called the penalty area.
terms.heard: "Get it in the box!" whenever a cross is coming.
terms.sayIt: "Get it in the box, someone!"
terms.overheard: Get it in the box. Stop passing it sideways.
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: The big rectangle in front of each goal
decoys: The dugout where the manager and subs sit
The six-yard area a keeper kicks from

terms.meaning: Kicking, tripping, pushing or holding another player. The referee blows, the other team gets a free kick, and if it was bad enough a card follows.
terms.heard: "That's a foul!", shouted most often by the side that has just lost the ball.
terms.sayIt: "That's a foul, surely. He went straight through him."
terms.overheard: Foul, ref! Are you watching the same game as me?
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: Going through the man, not the ball
decoys: A decision the referee got wrong
Arguing with the referee after a decision

terms.meaning: Touching the ball with your hand or arm on purpose, or with an arm stuck out making you bigger. Goalkeepers can use their hands, but only inside their own box.
terms.heard: "That's handball all day" about a ball that brushed a shoulder.
terms.sayIt: "His arm was out. That's handball."
terms.overheard: handball there surely. how has he not given that?
terms.speaker: chat
terms.gist: Touching the ball with an arm on purpose
decoys: The keeper picking the ball up outside his box
Grabbing an opponent's shirt to hold him back

terms.meaning: A restart after a foul: the ball is put down and kicked from where the foul happened. Near the goal, it is a chance to score.
terms.heard: "That's a free kick every day of the week."
terms.sayIt: "That's a free kick all day long."
terms.overheard: That's a free kick, surely. He's gone through the back of him.
terms.speaker: pundit
terms.gist: A restart taken from where the offence happened
decoys: A kick awarded for a foul inside the box
A drop ball restart after a player's hurt

terms.meaning: If a defender puts the ball out behind his own goal, the attackers get to cross it in from the corner of the pitch. Tall players love them.
terms.heard: "Corners are as good as a goal" said hopefully.
terms.sayIt: "Corner. Get everyone in the box."
terms.overheard: Corner. Get the big lads up, this is our chance.
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: A kick from the flag after a defender puts it out
decoys: A cross from deep while the ball is live
A free kick given wide, level with the goal

terms.meaning: Ball goes out over the sideline, the other team throws it back in, two hands, from behind the head.
terms.heard: Rarely. Unless someone has a famously long one.
terms.sayIt: "Long throw. They'll launch it into the box."
terms.overheard: Throw-in to them, deep inside their own half.
terms.speaker: telly
terms.gist: Putting the ball back in from the sideline
decoys: Giving up and letting the other lot have it
A free kick given out on the touchline

terms.meaning: Playing with one fewer after a red card. Teams usually drop back and defend for their lives.
terms.heard: "Down to ten men" said either with dread or delight.
terms.sayIt: "Down to ten men. Just hang on now."
terms.overheard: Ten men and we're somehow level here. Unbelievable.
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: A man down for the rest of the match
decoys: The ten outfield players, not the keeper
A shape with nobody up front

terms.meaning: Letting in no goals in a match. The goalkeeper's favourite statistic, and a defender's.
terms.heard: "Another clean sheet" said with real pride.
terms.sayIt: "Another clean sheet. The defence has been solid."
terms.overheard: Another clean sheet, and we didn't half ride our luck.
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: Letting in no goals at all in a match
decoys: A game with no cards and no trouble
Winning without conceding a penalty

terms.meaning: A match between two local rivals, usually from the same city. Pronounced darby. The week is tense before, during and after.
terms.heard: The week before, the week of, and the week after.
terms.sayIt: "It's the derby this weekend, isn't it? Are you nervous?"
terms.overheard: derby weekend. nobody book anything sunday, im no use after.
terms.speaker: chat
terms.gist: A match between two clubs from the same city
decoys: Any game with a real edge to it
A fixture played every year on the same day

terms.meaning: VAR is only meant to overturn a decision that was obviously wrong, not one that is debatable. The longer the check, the less obvious it was.
terms.heard: "If it takes that long it isn't clear and obvious."
terms.sayIt: "If it takes this long it's not clear and obvious, is it?"
terms.overheard: They keep saying clear and obvious. I've stopped believing in it.
terms.speaker: pundit
terms.gist: A decision so wrong nobody could argue
decoys: Footage good enough to see it
A decision the referee got right first time

terms.meaning: The second division, one below the Premier League. Confusing name: winning it does not make you champions of anything much.
terms.heard: "They'll be in the Championship next year" said unkindly.
terms.sayIt: "Is that a Championship side? So they came up recently."
terms.overheard: He's a Championship player at this level, I'm afraid.
terms.speaker: pundit
terms.gist: The division below the top one in England
decoys: A league for clubs' reserve and youth sides
The tier where the clubs are part-time

terms.meaning: In the Championship the top two go up automatically. The next four play a mini knockout for the third place. One final, one winner, one very rich club.
terms.heard: Late May. The final is called the richest game in football.
terms.sayIt: "Did they go up automatically or through the play-offs?"
terms.overheard: Play-offs again. I can't go through that a third year running.
terms.speaker: telly
terms.gist: A mini knockout deciding who goes up
decoys: A one-off final for the title
Extra games to decide who avoids going down

terms.meaning: Minutes added at the end of each half to make up for stoppages: injuries, substitutions, celebrations. Shown on a board by the pitch.
terms.heard: "How long has he added?" the second the board goes up.
terms.sayIt: "How long's he added? Six? Six minutes!"
terms.overheard: Six minutes of added time. Where has he got that from?
terms.speaker: telly
terms.gist: Extra play at the end for stoppages
decoys: A count of how long the ball was out of play
Time carried over from the first half

terms.meaning: Two extra fifteen-minute halves when a cup game is level. Not the same as added time. League games never have it; they just end as a draw.
terms.heard: In knockout games only.
terms.sayIt: "It's going to extra time. Put the kettle on."
terms.overheard: Extra time it is, then. Nobody wanted that.
terms.speaker: pundit
terms.gist: Half an hour more to settle a cup game
decoys: A short break before penalties are taken
The same round played again a week later

terms.meaning: If extra time is still level: five penalties each, then one at a time until somebody misses. Pure nerves.
terms.heard: England fans go quiet at the mention of it.
terms.sayIt: "Penalties. I can't watch penalties."
terms.overheard: penalty shootout. i cant look, text me when its done.
terms.speaker: chat
terms.gist: A round of five spot kicks each, then sudden death
decoys: One kick each until somebody misses
A free shot from twelve yards during play

terms.meaning: Knockout competitions run alongside the league: the FA Cup and the League Cup. Lose once and you are out of it for the season.
terms.heard: "It's only the cup" when they lose, "a cup run" when they win.
terms.sayIt: "Is this the league or the cup?"
terms.overheard: He never takes the cups seriously and it shows.
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: The knockout competitions beside the league
decoys: The trophies handed out at the end of a season
The two European competitions played midweek

terms.meaning: The oldest cup competition in the world, since 1871. Every club in England can enter, so tiny teams sometimes get to play giants. Final at Wembley in May.
terms.heard: "The magic of the cup" when a small club wins.
terms.sayIt: "FA Cup weekend. Any giant-killings on?"
terms.overheard: FA Cup third round. This is the one he wants.
terms.speaker: telly
terms.gist: The oldest knockout, open to every club
decoys: The competition every club in Europe can enter
The cup for the top two divisions

terms.meaning: The League Cup (Carabao Cup) is the smaller of the two domestic cups, so it takes the name of whichever sponsor is paying. Semi-finals over two legs, final at Wembley.
terms.heard: "Good chance to rest people" from the manager.
terms.sayIt: "It's only the League Cup. He'll rest half the team."
terms.overheard: It's the League Cup, and the sponsors have changed the name again.
terms.speaker: pundit
terms.gist: The smaller of the two domestic cups
decoys: A trophy for the winners of the division
The pre-season tournament played in August

terms.meaning: England's national stadium, in north-west London. Both domestic cup finals are played there, and the FA Cup semi-finals too. Ninety thousand seats under an arch.
terms.heard: "A trip to Wembley" means the cup run has gone deep.
terms.sayIt: "So a win here is a trip to Wembley?"
terms.overheard: Two games from Wembley. Don't say it out loud, don't jinx it.
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: The national stadium in north-west London
decoys: The name fans give to the cup final itself
The training base the national team uses

terms.meaning: Europe's top club competition. The best clubs from each country, midweek nights, that anthem before kick-off.
terms.heard: Tuesday and Wednesday nights, September to May.
terms.sayIt: "Champions League night. What time's kick-off?"
terms.overheard: That anthem, those lights. Champions League football is back.
terms.speaker: telly
terms.gist: Europe's top club competition
decoys: A competition for the winners of each division
The summer tournament between national sides

terms.meaning: Europe's second competition, for clubs that finished just below the Champions League places. Thursday nights.
terms.heard: "Thursday night football" said with a slight sigh.
terms.sayIt: "Thursday night football. Is that the Europa League?"
terms.overheard: Europa League on Thursday. I'll be up late again.
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: Europe's second club competition
decoys: The knockout stage of Europe's top competition
A tournament for national sides in Europe

terms.meaning: Europe's third competition, below the Champions League and the Europa League. Thursday nights, smaller clubs, and a real trophy for whoever wins it.
terms.heard: Thursday nights, often alongside the Europa League.
terms.sayIt: "Is that the Europa League or the Conference League?"
terms.overheard: conference league away trip in november. whos coming?
terms.speaker: chat
terms.gist: Europe's third club competition
decoys: A division below the Football League
The qualifying round before a group stage

terms.meaning: The list of upcoming matches: who plays who, when, and where. Published in June for the whole season.
terms.heard: "Have you seen the fixtures?" in June, when they come out.
terms.sayIt: "What's the next fixture? Home or away?"
terms.overheard: Fixtures are out. I've already booked three days off.
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: Who plays who, and when
decoys: Dates the tickets go on sale
The TV picks for the weekend's games

terms.meaning: The eleven players who begin the match. Announced about an hour before kick-off, when phones come out.
terms.heard: "Team's out" when the line-up appears on his phone.
terms.sayIt: "Team's out. Who's starting?"
terms.overheard: Team's up. Same starting eleven again, he's not learning.
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: The players picked to begin the match
decoys: The order the players run out in
The squad named for a European round

terms.meaning: Swapping a player on the pitch for one from the bench. Five changes allowed per game since 2022; it used to be three.
terms.heard: "Bit early for a sub" or "About time."
terms.sayIt: "Bit early for a sub, isn't it?"
terms.overheard: First substitution already, and it's half an hour gone.
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: Swapping a player on the pitch for one waiting
decoys: Taking a player off with nobody coming on
One player moving to cover another's role

terms.meaning: The substitutes, sitting beside the pitch waiting to come on. A strong bench means good players in reserve.
terms.heard: "He's on the bench" means not starting, but might play.
terms.sayIt: "He's only on the bench today? Is he injured?"
terms.overheard: hes on the bench again. third game running now…
terms.speaker: chat
terms.gist: The substitutes waiting beside the pitch
decoys: The staff sat in the dugout
The players left out of the squad entirely

terms.meaning: A cup round played as two matches, one at each ground. First leg, second leg. Neither result decides anything on its own; the two added together do.
terms.heard: "The second leg is at home" is good news.
terms.sayIt: "Is this the first leg or the second?"
terms.overheard: Remember, this is over two legs. Anything can happen from here.
terms.speaker: telly
terms.gist: One round played as two matches, home and away
decoys: The two halves either side of the break
A round decided by a second match if it's level

terms.meaning: Over two legs, add the two scores together. Win the first 2-0, lose the second 1-0, and you go through 2-1 on aggregate. The total is what counts.
terms.heard: European nights. "They're 3-2 up on aggregate."
terms.sayIt: "So what's the aggregate? Who's actually ahead?"
terms.overheard: The aggregate is all that matters now. Forget the performance.
terms.speaker: pundit
terms.gist: Both scores added together over a round
decoys: A club's goals across a season
The gap between goals scored and let in

terms.meaning: Putting the ball into your own net. It counts for the other team, and it follows the player around for years.
terms.heard: A pained "oh no" from the whole room.
terms.sayIt: "Oh no. Own goal. Poor lad."
terms.overheard: And that's an own goal. The second of the afternoon.
terms.speaker: telly
terms.gist: A ball put into your own net by mistake
decoys: A goal you score on your own, unassisted
A goal that came off a defender on the way in

terms.meaning: The pass that leads directly to a goal. The scorer gets the headline, the assist gets the credit from people who know.
terms.heard: "Goals and assists" when he's rating a player.
terms.sayIt: "Lovely assist. The pass was the best bit."
terms.overheard: Another assist for him. He's having a season.
terms.speaker: pundit
terms.gist: The pass that leads straight to a goal
decoys: Any pass in the move that led to the goal
Winning the ball back to start an attack

terms.meaning: Two goals by the same player in one match. Three is a hat-trick. There is no special word for four.
terms.heard: "He got a brace" in the match report.
terms.sayIt: "That's his brace. One more for a hat-trick."
terms.overheard: hes got a brace already and its not even half-time.
terms.speaker: chat
terms.gist: Two goals by the same player in a match
decoys: A strapping worn on a knee or ankle
One goal and one assist in a match

terms.meaning: Three goals by one player in one match. Two is a brace. The player traditionally keeps the match ball.
terms.heard: For days afterwards.
terms.sayIt: "Hat-trick! He's taking the ball home."
terms.overheard: That's the hat-trick, then. What a way to spend a Saturday.
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: Three goals by one man in a match
decoys: Three wins on the bounce for a club
Three goals for a side inside one half

terms.meaning: The best player on the day, picked by the broadcaster or a sponsor. A safe question to ask any fan.
terms.heard: "Who's your man of the match?" is a safe question every time.
terms.sayIt: "Who's your man of the match?"
terms.overheard: They've got man of the match wrong again, you know.
terms.speaker: pundit
terms.gist: The player judged best on the day
decoys: The supporters' player of the season
The player who speaks to the cameras after

terms.meaning: No goals for either side. Football says nil, not zero. A dull one is a bore draw.
terms.heard: "Bore draw" if it was dull, "a tight game" if he's being kind.
terms.sayIt: "Nil-nil. Bit of a bore draw, that."
terms.overheard: Nil-nil, that. He'll be in a mood all night.
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: Nobody scored, the match finished level
decoys: The game was abandoned, so no score counts
A draw where both sides scored

terms.meaning: Any restart from a dead ball: corners, free kicks, throw-ins. Teams rehearse them in training all week.
terms.heard: "Strong from set pieces" about tall teams.
terms.sayIt: "They're strong from set pieces. Watch the corners."
terms.overheard: They're a threat from set pieces, this lot. Always have been.
terms.speaker: pundit
terms.gist: A rehearsed routine from a dead ball
decoys: The eleven a manager settles on for a game
A goal that comes straight from open play

terms.meaning: How the ten outfield players line up, read from the back. 4-3-3 means four defenders, three midfielders, three attackers. The goalkeeper is never counted.
terms.heard: "They've gone 4-4-2" as if it explains everything.
terms.sayIt: "What formation are they playing? Looks like a back three."
terms.overheard: Changed the formation again, has he. No wonder they look lost.
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: The shape the ten outfield players start in
decoys: The eleven he picks to start the match
The way they set up for corners and free kicks

terms.meaning: The four defenders in a line in front of the goalkeeper: two centre-backs in the middle, a full-back on each side.
terms.heard: "The back four were solid" is high praise.
terms.sayIt: "The back four have been solid today."
terms.overheard: Same back four again. He's not changing that in a hurry.
terms.speaker: telly
terms.gist: The defenders in a line in front of the goalkeeper
decoys: The players sitting furthest back on the bench
The four across the middle of the pitch

terms.meaning: The two big defenders in the middle. Heading, tackling, shouting at everyone else.
terms.heard: "He's a proper centre-back" means old-fashioned and tough.
terms.sayIt: "He's a proper centre-back. Wins every header."
terms.overheard: We've spent a fortune on that centre-back. Jury's out for me.
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: A defender in the middle who wins headers
decoys: A midfielder who shields the defence behind him
The one who whips the crosses in from wide

terms.meaning: The defenders on the left and right who also sprint forward to attack. Busiest job on the pitch.
terms.heard: "The full-backs were up and down all day."
terms.sayIt: "The full-backs have been up and down all game."
terms.overheard: Both full-backs are booked now. That's a worry with an hour to go.
terms.speaker: pundit
terms.gist: A defender out wide who also joins the attack
decoys: An attacker who hugs the touchline all game
A defender who plays the whole ninety every week

terms.meaning: A full-back who plays higher up the pitch, almost as a winger, because there are three centre-backs behind him.
terms.heard: When a team plays with a back three.
terms.sayIt: "They're playing wing-backs today, so it's a back three."
terms.overheard: He's gone with wing-backs today. That's bold against this lot.
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: A wide defender pushed up almost as an attacker
decoys: A back-up who covers out wide when needed
A midfielder who stays out on the touchline

terms.meaning: The midfielder who stays back and protects the defence instead of running forward. Unglamorous, essential.
terms.heard: "The six" or "the number six", after the shirt number they used to wear.
terms.sayIt: "Who's playing the holding role? He's not getting forward."
terms.overheard: They need a proper holding midfielder. That's been the problem all season.
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: The one who sits in front of the defence
decoys: A player told to hold on to the ball
The one who plays just behind the striker

terms.meaning: A midfielder who runs from his own penalty area to the other one all game. Defends, attacks, never stops.
terms.heard: "Proper box-to-box midfielder" said admiringly.
terms.sayIt: "He's a proper box-to-box player. Everywhere."
terms.overheard: He's box-to-box, that lad. Doesn't half make it look easy.
terms.speaker: chat
terms.gist: A midfielder who runs the length of the pitch
decoys: The one who pings it from one box to the other
A midfielder who gets forward to score goals

terms.meaning: The creative player just behind the striker who makes the clever passes. Named after the shirt number the best of them wore.
terms.heard: "He's a classic ten" about someone who can't be bothered to defend.
terms.sayIt: "He's playing as the ten today, just behind the striker."
terms.overheard: He's the number ten tonight. A big call from the manager, that.
terms.speaker: telly
terms.gist: The creative one just off the front man
decoys: The player wearing the shirt with ten on
The one the manager picks as captain

terms.meaning: The player everything goes through. Sees passes nobody else sees. Stop him and you stop the team.
terms.heard: "He makes them tick" is the phrase.
terms.sayIt: "He's the one who makes them tick."
terms.overheard: Their playmaker was at it again tonight. He's some player, him.
terms.speaker: pundit
terms.gist: The one every attack goes through
decoys: The one who takes the corners and free kicks
The one who barks the orders at everyone

terms.meaning: An attacker who plays out wide near the touchline, runs at defenders and crosses the ball in.
terms.heard: "Get it wide to the winger!"
terms.sayIt: "Get it out wide! The winger's in space."
terms.overheard: That winger has had a stinker tonight. Not been in it at all.
terms.speaker: chat
terms.gist: An attacker who runs at people wide
decoys: The forward who plays just off the striker
A defender who gets forward down the touchline

terms.meaning: The player whose whole job is scoring goals. Also called a forward, a centre-forward or a number nine.
terms.heard: "They need a striker" about half the clubs in the league.
terms.sayIt: "They need a proper striker, don't they?"
terms.overheard: Two years we've been after a striker. Two years.
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: The one up front whose job is scoring
decoys: The one who strikes the dead balls for them
The player who plays behind the front man

terms.meaning: A big striker the team aims long balls at. He holds the ball up and brings others into play.
terms.heard: "Get it up to the big man" when a team is desperate.
terms.sayIt: "Just get it up to the big man."
terms.overheard: You need a target man in this league. They've not got one.
terms.speaker: pundit
terms.gist: A big forward the ball gets launched at
decoys: A defender told to follow one player about
A forward who chases everything down

terms.meaning: A striker who drops back into midfield instead of staying up front, so the defenders don't know who to mark.
terms.heard: In clever tactical chats. Sounds fancier than it is.
terms.sayIt: "He's playing as a false nine, dropping into midfield."
terms.overheard: He's playing a false nine there. We'll see how long that lasts.
terms.speaker: telly
terms.gist: A forward who drops deep to confuse markers
decoys: A player faking an injury to waste some time
A forward told to stay high on the shoulder

terms.meaning: Changing several players between matches to keep legs fresh. In an early League Cup round a manager might make eight changes and hand the young lads a game.
terms.heard: "He's rotating" when the line-up looks unfamiliar.
terms.sayIt: "He's rotated half the side. It's only the League Cup."
terms.overheard: Rotation, he's calling it. I'm not convinced, me.
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: Changing several players to rest legs
decoys: Players taking turns as captain in a season
Swapping positions with someone mid-match

terms.meaning: Chasing the opponent the moment he gets the ball, all over the pitch, to force a mistake. Exhausting when it works and when it doesn't.
terms.heard: "They press really well" about energetic teams.
terms.sayIt: "They press so well. Nobody gets a second on the ball."
terms.overheard: It's all about the pressing with this manager. Nothing else matters.
terms.speaker: pundit
terms.gist: Hounding whoever has it into a mistake
decoys: Newspapers and TV crowding round the club
Playing the ball forward at every chance

terms.meaning: Pressing right up near the other team's goal, so they can't even pass the ball out from their own defence.
terms.heard: When a team wins the ball near the corner flag and scores.
terms.sayIt: "The high press won them that. Forced the mistake."
terms.overheard: He's gone with the high press today. That's a big risk, that.
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: Winning it back right on top of their keeper
decoys: Launching the ball up in the air and chasing
Sitting deep and waiting for a chance to break

terms.meaning: The whole team sitting deep near their own goal, letting the other side have the ball and hoping to hit them on the counter.
terms.heard: "They've sat in a low block" about a team defending a lead.
terms.sayIt: "They're sitting in a low block. Someone needs to unlock it."
terms.overheard: They've gone to a low block now. This'll be a long old night.
terms.speaker: telly
terms.gist: Defending deep, letting the other lot have it
decoys: Playing with three at the back instead of four
Dropping the back line deep to protect a win

terms.meaning: Defending with everyone and attacking with nobody, as if a bus were parked across the goal. Usually to protect a lead.
terms.heard: Usually as an insult about a boring opponent.
terms.sayIt: "They've parked the bus. This'll be hard work."
terms.overheard: They've parked the bus since that goal. Forty minutes of this left.
terms.speaker: pundit
terms.gist: Everyone back defending, nobody trying to attack
decoys: Wasting time at every throw-in and free kick
Bringing defenders on to hang on to a lead

terms.meaning: Winning the ball and racing up the pitch fast before the other team can get back into position.
terms.heard: "Dangerous on the counter" about quick teams.
terms.sayIt: "They're dangerous on the counter. Don't push too many forward."
terms.overheard: They're built for the counter-attack, this lot. It's no accident.
terms.speaker: chat
terms.gist: Breaking forward fast the second you win it
decoys: Scoring straight back after going behind
Pushing everyone forward chasing a late goal

terms.meaning: How much of the game a team has the ball, shown as a percentage. Having it is nice; scoring is better.
terms.heard: "Sixty percent possession and nothing to show for it."
terms.sayIt: "All that possession and nothing to show for it."
terms.overheard: He's obsessed with the possession. It tells you nothing, that.
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: The share of the game a side has the ball
decoys: The number of times a side touches the ball
The count of shots each side has on target

terms.meaning: Lots of short, quick passes to keep the ball and wear the other team out. Barcelona and Spain made it famous.
terms.heard: Half in praise, half in mockery.
terms.sayIt: "Bit of tiki-taka there. Nobody can get near them."
terms.overheard: Loads of tiki-taka tonight. Not a lot else happening, mind.
terms.speaker: chat
terms.gist: Endless short passes to keep hold of the ball
decoys: The chant the away end sings on repeat
A quick one-two played round a defender

terms.meaning: Kicking the ball high and far up the pitch instead of passing it along the ground. Simple, direct, unloved.
terms.heard: "Route one" is the same idea, said more rudely.
terms.sayIt: "Long ball again. Not pretty, but it works."
terms.overheard: Another long ball. That's his way, always has been.
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: Hitting it high and far instead of passing
decoys: A shot struck from forty yards or further
The cross whipped in low from the byline

terms.meaning: The simplest way to attack: kick it long and chase it. Named after the most direct road.
terms.heard: As an insult about direct teams.
terms.sayIt: "Route one. Not pretty, is it?"
terms.overheard: Proper route one stuff, this. Not for me.
terms.speaker: pundit
terms.gist: Kicking it long and chasing it, no build-up
decoys: Working the ball wide and crossing it
Passing it through the middle at speed

terms.meaning: A defender following one particular attacker everywhere he goes, rather than guarding an area.
terms.heard: "Who's marking him?" after a free header.
terms.sayIt: "Who was marking him? He was completely free."
terms.overheard: They've gone man-marking today. You don't see that often.
terms.speaker: telly
terms.gist: Sticking with one opponent all game
decoys: Each defender covering an area of the pitch
Standing goal-side of your man at a corner

terms.meaning: At corners and free kicks, each defender guards a patch of ground instead of a person. Blamed for every goal from a corner.
terms.heard: Blamed for every goal from a corner.
terms.sayIt: "Zonal marking. Nobody's actually on anyone."
terms.overheard: That's zonal marking for you. I've no time for it.
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: Each defender guards a patch of grass
decoys: Switching off and losing concentration
The wall lined up in front of a free kick

terms.meaning: A full-back running past the winger on the outside to give him someone to pass to.
terms.heard: "Great overlap" from a co-commentator.
terms.sayIt: "Lovely overlap from the full-back there."
terms.overheard: He's missed the overlap again. That's twice in five minutes.
terms.speaker: telly
terms.gist: A defender running outside his winger
decoys: A pass rolled inside instead of out wide
A player drifting into a teammate's space

terms.meaning: A pass slid between the defenders for a teammate to run onto. When it works it looks like magic.
terms.heard: "What a ball" when it works.
terms.sayIt: "What a ball! Straight through them."
terms.overheard: Just look at that through ball. Wonderful, that.
terms.speaker: telly
terms.gist: A pass slid between two defenders
decoys: A ball nudged past a player's legs
A cross aimed at the far post

terms.meaning: Getting to the byline and passing the ball back across the goal for someone to tap in. Modern teams score half their goals this way.
terms.heard: Modern teams score half their goals this way.
terms.sayIt: "Cut it back! Don't shoot from there."
terms.overheard: Another cutback. They score all their goals like that.
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: A pass pulled square from the byline
decoys: A player turning inside to lose a marker
A cross floated to the far post

terms.meaning: A full-back who steps into midfield when his team has the ball, to give them an extra passer in the middle.
terms.heard: Guardiola fans. Sounds very clever.
terms.sayIt: "The full-back's inverting. He's basically a midfielder now."
terms.overheard: They've gone to inverted full-backs. It's all a bit much for me.
terms.speaker: pundit
terms.gist: A wide defender stepping into midfield
decoys: A defender playing on the opposite side
A midfielder dropping in among the defence

terms.meaning: The gap between the middle of the pitch and the wing, where clever attackers like to get the ball because nobody is quite sure who marks them.
terms.heard: Tactics podcasts. Nod if you hear it.
terms.sayIt: "He keeps finding space in the half-space. Nobody picks him up."
terms.overheard: He lives in the half-space, that lad. It's a podcast word, apparently.
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: The lane between the middle and the touchline
decoys: The half of the pitch a side sets up to defend
The strip of grass right in front of the goal mouth

terms.meaning: Expected goals. A number for how good a chance was: a tap-in is nearly 1, a shot from forty yards is nearly 0. Add them up to see who deserved to win.
terms.heard: "The xG was 2.5 and we lost 1-0" as a complaint.
terms.sayIt: "What was the xG? Felt like they should've scored three."
terms.overheard: Have a look at the xG from that. It'll only wind you up.
terms.speaker: chat
terms.gist: A score for how good a chance was
decoys: How many goals a side should score in a season
The shots on target added up

terms.meaning: Slowing the match down when you are winning: keeping the ball, taking your time, no risks. Called clever by the winners and cynical by the losers.
terms.heard: "Good game management" or "cynical", depending on who's winning.
terms.sayIt: "Good game management. Just keep the ball now."
terms.overheard: That's game management, apparently. Dull as you like, this.
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: Slowing it down to protect a lead
decoys: The manager barking at them from the side
Changing the shape after an hour

terms.meaning: Hold onto a lead until the final whistle without anything going wrong. The hardest ten minutes in football.
terms.heard: "Just see it out" in the last ten minutes.
terms.sayIt: "Just see the game out now. Nothing silly."
terms.overheard: They just need to see the game out from here.
terms.speaker: telly
terms.gist: Protect a lead until the final whistle
decoys: Stay on the pitch without getting sent off
Push for another goal to settle it

terms.meaning: The nervous final minutes when your team is only just ahead and the other lot are pushing. Fans shift about in plastic seats, hence the squeak. Alex Ferguson's phrase.
terms.heard: The last ten minutes of anything close.
terms.sayIt: "Right, squeaky bum time. I can't watch."
terms.overheard: Squeaky bum time now. Don't talk to me.
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: The jitters as the clock winds down
decoys: The bit where players start time-wasting
The nervous wait while a goal is checked

terms.meaning: The sneaky side of winning: time-wasting, little fouls, winding opponents up. Fans hate it from the other team and defend it from their own.
terms.heard: "Bit of the dark arts" said with grudging respect.
terms.sayIt: "Bit of the dark arts there. Fair play, it's working."
terms.overheard: Proper dark arts from this lot tonight. Been at it for years.
terms.speaker: chat
terms.gist: The sneaky stuff that winds them up
decoys: Playing a weakened side on purpose
Rough tackling meant to rattle them

terms.meaning: Attacking fast right after winning the ball, the same as a counter-attack.
terms.heard: "They caught them on the break."
terms.sayIt: "They got caught on the break there."
terms.overheard: They'll hurt you on the break, this lot. Watch.
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: Attacking at speed before they can get back
decoys: Scoring right after the half-time interval
Winning the ball high up the pitch

terms.meaning: Kick the ball as hard and far as you can with no real aim, usually to get it away from danger. Not elegant. Sometimes exactly right.
terms.heard: "Just hoof it!" from the sofa when the defence is under pressure.
terms.sayIt: "Just hoof it! Get it out of there."
terms.overheard: Just hoof it! He's under pressure there.
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: Boot the ball clear with no particular aim
decoys: Knock it back to the keeper to start again
Put it out of play to stop the attack

terms.meaning: The back row of the stand. Where a shot goes when it is blazed miles over, or where a defender deliberately hoofs the ball to safety.
terms.heard: "That's in Row Z" about a shot that nearly hit the roof.
terms.sayIt: "Row Z. He's ballooned that."
terms.overheard: He's put that in Row Z. He'll not want to see that again.
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: The back of the stand, where a wild shot lands
decoys: A shot that clears the crossbar by inches
The seats behind the goal at either end

terms.meaning: Launching the ball into the crowded penalty box and hoping. Late-game desperation, and sometimes it works.
terms.heard: "Just get it in the mixer" in the last minute.
terms.sayIt: "Get it in the mixer! Anything now."
terms.overheard: Get it in the mixer! Stop faffing about.
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: Launching the ball into a crowded penalty area
decoys: Getting it wide to the winger to cross
Booting it into the corner to run the clock

terms.meaning: After a header or a clearance, the loose ball that drops. Winning the second ball means reacting quickest to it.
terms.heard: "They won the second ball" as praise for hard work.
terms.sayIt: "They keep winning the second ball. That's why they're on top."
terms.overheard: It's all about the second ball, this.
terms.speaker: telly
terms.gist: Whatever drops loose after a header
decoys: A cross played in after a short corner
The second goal that settles a match

terms.meaning: An easy chance that should have been a goal and wasn't. The kind you would score yourself, you tell him.
terms.heard: "How has he missed that?"
terms.sayIt: "That's a sitter. How has he missed that?"
terms.overheard: He's missed a sitter there. I've seen enough.
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: A chance so easy it should have been a goal
decoys: A shot dragged wide from a tight angle
A shot the keeper palms away at full stretch

terms.meaning: A cool, precise shot that goes exactly where it should. Nothing spectacular, nothing wasted. The scorer is a clinical finisher.
terms.heard: Commentators, about a striker who never seems to miss.
terms.sayIt: "Clinical. Absolutely clinical finish."
terms.overheard: That's clinical finishing. He'll sleep well tonight.
terms.speaker: pundit
terms.gist: A calm, precise shot that beats the keeper
decoys: A goal that takes a big deflection
A move drilled on the training ground

terms.meaning: A spectacular goal, usually hit very hard from a long way out. Followed by a replay, then another.
terms.heard: "What a screamer" and then the replay, twice.
terms.sayIt: "What a screamer! Show me that again."
terms.overheard: And that is a screamer. Get the replay on.
terms.speaker: telly
terms.gist: A goal hit very hard from a long way out
decoys: A shot that flies well over the bar
A goal that settles a nervy game late on

terms.meaning: The top corner of the goal. The hardest place for a keeper to reach and the nicest place to score.
terms.heard: "Top bins!" with real joy.
terms.sayIt: "Top bins! Keeper had no chance."
terms.overheard: TOP BINS. Oh, that's filthy, that is.
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: A corner of the goal no keeper can reach
decoys: A shot that creeps in off the inside of the post
A shot the keeper gets a hand to and can't stop

terms.meaning: A world-class goal. Short for world-class. Save it for the truly special ones or it loses its power.
terms.heard: Only for the very best ones.
terms.sayIt: "That's a worldie. Goal of the season, that."
terms.overheard: Worldie, that. I've watched it four times.
terms.speaker: chat
terms.gist: A goal of genuine world-class quality
decoys: A goal scored at the World Cup
A goal that wins goal of the month

terms.meaning: Excellent. A top-drawer pass, a top-drawer save. Pundit English for very, very good.
terms.heard: Pundits, about anything they liked.
terms.sayIt: "Top drawer, that. Absolute quality."
terms.overheard: He's top drawer, that lad. Always has been.
terms.speaker: pundit
terms.gist: Excellent, the very highest quality
decoys: The top division of English football
A player kept back for the big games

terms.meaning: The ball strikes the post or the crossbar and stays out. Close enough to hurt.
terms.heard: "Off the woodwork" with a groan from the whole room.
terms.sayIt: "Off the woodwork! So close."
terms.overheard: That's twice they've hit the woodwork. Not their day.
terms.speaker: telly
terms.gist: The ball struck the post or bar and stayed out
decoys: The ball smashed into the boards behind the goal
A shot that beat the keeper and went wide

terms.meaning: What fans shout at a player who has just missed. Means nothing and everything.
terms.heard: Shouted at a player who has just missed.
terms.sayIt: "Unlucky! Keep going."
terms.overheard: Unlucky! Oh, for crying out loud.
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: A shout of sympathy at a player who missed
decoys: A groan when the keeper makes a save
A shout at the referee for a poor call

terms.meaning: Poking the ball between a defender's legs and running round him to collect it. Humiliating for the defender, hilarious for everyone else.
terms.heard: A cheer that has nothing to do with a goal.
terms.sayIt: "Nutmeg! He'll never live that down."
terms.overheard: He's nutmegged him and the ground's gone up.
terms.speaker: telly
terms.gist: Knocking the ball through a defender's legs
decoys: Barging a defender off the ball and going past
Flicking the ball over a defender's head

terms.meaning: Got past a defender so completely he was left standing. Skinned him and left him for dead mean the same.
terms.heard: "He's done him" after a dribble.
terms.sayIt: "He's done him there. Left him for dead."
terms.overheard: He's done him there. Watch the replay of that.
terms.speaker: chat
terms.gist: Leaving a defender standing
decoys: Fouling an opponent on purpose
Rounding the keeper and walking it in

terms.meaning: A defender switching off for a second and letting an attacker get free. Also called going to sleep.
terms.heard: "Caught napping" or "gone to sleep" after a goal against.
terms.sayIt: "They were caught napping there. Nobody was awake."
terms.overheard: Caught napping again, that lot. Dear me.
terms.speaker: pundit
terms.gist: Switching off and letting an attacker get free
decoys: Losing a header to a much taller player
Being caught too high up when it turns over

terms.meaning: A goal for the team that has been playing worse. They were being battered, then scored anyway.
terms.heard: Commentators, when the wrong team scores.
terms.sayIt: "That's against the run of play. They've been terrible."
terms.overheard: That is against the run of play, no question.
terms.speaker: telly
terms.gist: A goal for the side who have been worse
decoys: A goal that came from a counter-attack
A goal scored in the closing minutes

terms.meaning: Winning a game you were outplayed in, with one late goal. A burglary, football-style.
terms.heard: Said by whichever side lost.
terms.sayIt: "Smash and grab, that. They didn't deserve it."
terms.overheard: Smash and grab, that. Typical of this lot.
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: A win in a match you were outplayed in
decoys: A tackle that takes the ball and the man
A late equaliser to rescue a point

terms.meaning: A terrible, obvious mistake, usually by a goalkeeper or defender: a ball through the hands, a pass straight to the opposition. Everyone saw it.
terms.heard: "Absolute howler" about a ball rolling under someone's foot.

terms.overheard: Absolute howler from the keeper. Have you seen it?
terms.speaker: chat
terms.gist: A glaring, embarrassing mistake
decoys: A save so good the crowd roared
A furious shout at his own defenders

terms.meaning: A careless pass that lands between two players from opposite sides, so both go for it and somebody gets hurt.
terms.heard: "That's a hospital ball" when a pass leaves a teammate exposed.
terms.sayIt: "Hospital ball, that. He's left him in trouble."
terms.overheard: That's a hospital ball. He can't be doing that at this level.
terms.speaker: pundit
terms.gist: A loose pass that leaves a teammate in trouble
decoys: A heavy touch that gives the ball away
A challenge bad enough to injure someone

terms.overheard: He's dived, ref! Are you watching this?

terms.gist: Falling over on purpose to win a foul

Sliding in feet first to win the ball

terms.meaning: Being sent off. The player heads to the showers while everyone else is still playing.

terms.sayIt: "Early bath for him. That was a proper tackle."
terms.overheard: That's an early bath for him, then. Silly boy.

terms.gist: Sent off, heading for the showers
decoys: Subbed off before he gets himself booked
Missing the next game as punishment

terms.meaning: A pushing and shoving scuffle between players that looks angry but never becomes a proper fight. Nobody gets hurt.

terms.sayIt: "Handbags. Nothing in that."
terms.overheard: Handbags at the corner flag. The ref's got a job on.

Players surrounding the referee in a group

terms.meaning: Booked. The referee writes the player's name in his notebook when he gives a yellow card.
terms.heard: "He's in the book" after a yellow card.
terms.sayIt: "He's in the book now. He'll have to be careful."
terms.overheard: He's in the book after four minutes. Calm down, lad.

terms.gist: The referee has shown him a yellow card
decoys: He has been sent off and must leave
The referee has spoken to him and let him off

terms.meaning: Substituted, usually because you were playing badly. Taken off, not rested.
terms.heard: "He's been hooked" about a player having a bad day.
terms.sayIt: "He's been hooked. Not his day."
terms.overheard: He's getting hooked here. He knows it, too.

terms.gist: Taken off for playing badly, not for a rest
decoys: Caught by an arm and pulled back illegally
Swapped out to save him for the next game

terms.meaning: Defending desperately with everyone behind the ball because the other team has all the pressure.
terms.heard: "Backs to the wall" in the last twenty minutes of a close game.
terms.sayIt: "Backs to the wall now. Just hang on."
terms.overheard: Backs to the wall for the home side, and the noise is up.

terms.gist: Soaking up heavy pressure near your own goal
decoys: Players lining up in a wall at a free-kick
Playing the ball back to the keeper to waste time

terms.meaning: The oldest cliché in football: a match that changed completely after half-time. Said half-jokingly, always.

terms.overheard: It's been a game of two halves, hasn't it?
terms.speaker: pundit
terms.gist: A match that turned after the break

A match where both sides scored twice

terms.overheard: Dead rubber tonight. I'll probably miss it.

terms.gist: A match with nothing riding on it any more

A match replayed after a draw

terms.overheard: Six-pointer on Saturday. Don't be planning anything.

terms.gist: A match between two sides chasing the same place

A game worth double because it is a derby

The scrap for a place in Europe

A run of hard games against the top clubs

The fee one club pays another for a player

terms.heard: Someone shouting "here we go" at a phone.
terms.sayIt: "Deadline day. Anything happening?"
terms.overheard: Deadline day, and we're outside the ground with nothing to tell you.
terms.speaker: telly
terms.gist: The final day for doing deals
decoys: The final day to buy tickets for the season
Cut-off for naming the squad for a cup

terms.meaning: Borrowing a player from another club for a season, or lending one out. Common for young players who need games.
terms.heard: "He's out on loan" about a promising kid.
terms.sayIt: "Is he ours or on loan?"
terms.overheard: He's gone out on loan for the season. Bit of a surprise.
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: Borrowing a player from another club for a while
decoys: Dropping down a division to get regular games
Playing for the reserve side until he's wanted

terms.meaning: The summer, when there is no football and every transfer rumour gets printed as if it were true.
terms.heard: "Ignore it, it's silly season" about a wild headline.
terms.sayIt: "Is that real or is it just silly season?"
terms.overheard: Silly season, that's all this is. Same every year.
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: Summer, when every rumour gets printed
decoys: The run of games over Christmas and New Year
A spell when results make no sense at all

terms.meaning: Transfer reporter Fabrizio Romano's phrase for a deal that is definitely happening. Fans wait for it like a verdict.
terms.heard: Screenshot in the group chat with several exclamation marks.
terms.sayIt: "Has Romano said here we go yet?"
terms.overheard: Here we go, apparently. My phone hasn't stopped.
terms.speaker: chat
terms.gist: The reporter's signal a transfer is done
decoys: The chant fans start as a big game kicks off
The countdown to the window shutting

terms.meaning: Fired. Managers get the sack when results go bad; players never do, they get sold or loaned out.
terms.heard: "He'll be sacked by Christmas" after three defeats.
terms.sayIt: "If they lose this, is he getting sacked?"
terms.overheard: hes getting sacked in the morning and about time too.
terms.speaker: chat
terms.gist: Losing the job when results go bad
decoys: A player dropped from the squad for a game
The manager walking out for a bigger club

terms.meaning: The unofficial contest for which manager gets fired first each season. Bookmakers take bets on it.
terms.heard: "He's favourite in the sack race" after three losses.
terms.sayIt: "Is he favourite in the sack race now?"
terms.overheard: He'll be in the sack race by Christmas at this rate.
terms.speaker: chat
terms.gist: The unofficial contest over which manager goes first
decoys: A charity event before a game at the ground
The run of games that decides a manager's future

terms.meaning: The short burst of good results a team often gets right after changing manager. It rarely lasts.
terms.heard: "Just the bounce" when a new manager wins his first two.
terms.sayIt: "Is that just the new manager bounce, or is he actually good?"
terms.overheard: You'll hear a lot about the new manager bounce this week.
terms.speaker: pundit
terms.gist: The short run of good results after a change
decoys: The lift in ticket sales after an appointment
The boost a home crowd gives a struggling side

terms.meaning: The manager. Old British slang for the boss, still used by players and fans.
terms.heard: "The gaffer's got them playing" from players and pundits alike.
terms.sayIt: "What's the gaffer like? Do the players rate him?"
terms.overheard: Gaffer's seen it. Look at his face.
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: The manager, in old workplace slang
decoys: The club captain who leads on the pitch
The head of the backroom staff at a club

terms.meaning: Also the manager. Players say it so they don't have to use his name in interviews.
terms.heard: Post-match interviews. "The boss said to keep going."
terms.sayIt: "The boss won't be happy with that."
terms.overheard: It'll be the boss's call and nobody will argue with it.
terms.speaker: pundit
terms.gist: The manager, the word the squad uses for him
decoys: The club owner who pays everyone's wages
The senior player who speaks in the dressing room

terms.meaning: A manager screaming at players at half-time from so close their hair moves. Named for Alex Ferguson, who was famous for it.
terms.heard: "They'll be getting the hairdryer" after a bad first half.
terms.sayIt: "They'll be getting the hairdryer at half-time."
terms.overheard: Hairdryer time in that dressing room, I bet.
terms.speaker: chat
terms.gist: A manager screaming at players up close
decoys: A calm team talk to settle everyone down
A row between players in the dressing room

terms.meaning: To lose your nerve at the crucial moment and throw away something you should have won. The cruellest word in a title race.
terms.heard: Cruelly, about title races that collapsed.
terms.sayIt: "Do you think they'll bottle it?"
terms.overheard: I'm saying nothing yet. We'll bottle it, we always do.
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: To lose your nerve at the crucial moment
decoys: To keep it all in and say nothing about it
To waste chances in front of goal all game

terms.meaning: The BBC's Saturday night highlights show, running since 1964. The theme tune alone makes fans sit up.
terms.heard: "Just watching MOTD" at 10.30pm on a Saturday.
terms.sayIt: "Are we watching Match of the Day tonight?"
terms.overheard: Match of the Day gets worse every year. I still watch it, mind.
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: The BBC's Saturday night highlights show
decoys: The televised game chosen for Saturday teatime
A round-up of the goals from abroad each week

terms.meaning: An ex-player who talks about the match on TV. Paid to have opinions, blamed for having them.
terms.heard: "He's a pundit now" about a player who retired.
terms.sayIt: "What did the pundits say about it?"
terms.overheard: The pundits said we'd be fine. That's the worry.
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: An ex-player paid to give opinions on TV
decoys: A journalist who writes the match report
An expert who predicts the score beforehand

terms.meaning: A pass for every home league game. Waiting lists at big clubs can be years long, and people inherit them.
terms.heard: "I've had a season ticket since I was eight."
terms.sayIt: "Have you ever had a season ticket?"
terms.overheard: My dad had that season ticket before me. No chance I'm giving it up.
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: A pass covering every home league game
decoys: A pass that gets you into any ground you like
A membership that lets you buy cup tickets early

terms.meaning: Travelling to watch the team at another ground. Trains, pubs, singing, and a long journey home if they lose.
terms.heard: "Big away day" when it's somewhere far or somewhere fun.
terms.sayIt: "Is it an away day? Who are you going with?"
terms.overheard: Big away day Saturday. I'll be useless by Sunday.
terms.speaker: chat
terms.gist: A trip to watch the team at another ground
decoys: A day off the players get away from the club
A pre-season friendly played overseas

terms.meaning: The section of the stadium where the travelling fans sit. Usually the loudest part of the ground.
terms.heard: "Listen to the away end" when the home fans have gone quiet.
terms.sayIt: "Listen to the away end. They're louder than the home fans."
terms.overheard: Second half and they're attacking the away end now.
terms.speaker: telly
terms.gist: The part of the ground given to visiting fans
decoys: The end of the pitch the visitors attack
The stand behind the goal at the far side

terms.meaning: The old standing areas at football grounds. Mostly seats now, but the word stuck for the fans and their songs.
terms.heard: "Terrace chant" about a song the crowd sings.
terms.sayIt: "That's a proper terrace chant, that."
terms.overheard: My old man swore by the terraces. He'd not enjoy it now.
terms.speaker: pundit
terms.gist: The old standing areas, and the fans in them
decoys: The rows of houses behind an old ground
The banked rows of seating in the top tier

terms.meaning: A song sung by the crowd, usually to a pop tune with new words about a player or the manager.
terms.heard: Him humming one in the kitchen.
terms.sayIt: "What's that chant they're singing? What are the words?"
terms.overheard: The whole ground was on that chant tonight. Goosebumps.
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: A song the crowd sings to a pop tune
decoys: A rhythm the crowd claps without words
The song a club plays as the teams come out

terms.meaning: Liverpool's famous home stand at Anfield, where the loudest fans sing. Other grounds borrowed the name for their own big stand.
terms.heard: Anfield nights on TV.
terms.sayIt: "Is that the Kop end? It's so loud."
terms.overheard: The Kop are on their feet and they've not sat down for ten minutes.
terms.speaker: telly
terms.gist: Liverpool's loud home stand at Anfield
decoys: The steepest old stand, where tickets are cheap
A stand named after a club's great manager

terms.meaning: A souvenir scarf with both teams' colours on it. Proper fans find them deeply embarrassing.
terms.heard: Mocked outside every big game.
terms.sayIt: "Please tell me you've never owned a half-and-half scarf."
terms.overheard: Bloke in front of us in a half-and-half scarf. Unbelievable scenes.
terms.speaker: chat
terms.gist: A souvenir showing both teams' colours
decoys: A ticket that covers both legs of a round
A scarf swapped with a rival fan at full time

terms.meaning: The team. How players and fans refer to their own side.
terms.heard: "Proud of the lads" after a hard game.
terms.sayIt: "The lads did well today."
terms.overheard: Buzzing for the lads tonight. Been a long few weeks.
terms.speaker: chat
terms.gist: The team, as the players and fans call it
decoys: The younger players coming through the academy
The travelling fans who follow every game

terms.meaning: Teasing between fans. Mostly friendly, occasionally not, always defended as "just banter".
terms.heard: "It's just banter" after a text that went slightly too far.
terms.sayIt: "Is that banter or are you actually annoyed?"
terms.overheard: He's not answered since Saturday. Can't take the banter.
terms.speaker: chat
terms.gist: Teasing between fans, mostly good-natured
decoys: Chatter between the players on the pitch
A row between fans that has gone too far

terms.meaning: Where his mates react to every goal in real time. Louder than the stadium and less forgiving.
terms.heard: His phone buzzing eleven times in a row after a goal.
terms.sayIt: "What's the group chat saying?"
terms.overheard: Don't mind me, I'm just catching up on the group chat.
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: Where his mates react to every goal instantly
decoys: An online forum open to all supporters
Fans posting videos from inside the ground

terms.meaning: Match of the Day's pick of the best goal, voted by viewers. Long-range strikes usually win.
terms.heard: "That's goal of the month" about any long-range strike.
terms.sayIt: "That's goal of the month, surely?"
terms.overheard: Goal of the month's going to be a tough one this time.
terms.speaker: pundit
terms.gist: The best strike, picked by a viewers' vote
decoys: The award for a player's form over four weeks
A scoring target a striker is set each month

terms.meaning: The linesman, now officially an assistant referee. The one with the flag who decides offsides.
terms.heard: "Lino!" shouted at a flag that went up or stayed down.
terms.sayIt: "The lino's flagged. Offside."
terms.overheard: Lino! That's never a throw to them. He's making it up now.
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: The assistant referee who judges offside
decoys: The painted markings around the pitch
The fourth official holding up the board

terms.meaning: The old joke about physios curing any injury with a wet sponge. Players hop up as if nothing happened.
terms.heard: Ironically, when a player recovers very quickly.
terms.sayIt: "Give him the magic sponge, he'll be fine."
terms.overheard: Here comes the magic sponge. We've all seen this before.
terms.speaker: telly
terms.gist: A wet flannel that fixes any knock
decoys: A cloth used to dry the ball
The stretcher carried on for a bad injury

terms.meaning: What players and fans say after a bad result. Move on, next match. Half slogan, half coping mechanism.
terms.heard: Player interviews after a defeat, and his text the morning after.
terms.sayIt: "One of those days. We go again."
terms.overheard: We go again Tuesday. Kick-off's at eight, apparently.
terms.speaker: chat
terms.gist: Bad result, forget it, on to the next game
decoys: The match is being replayed after a draw
Fans are heading off to another away trip

terms.meaning: Generous added time that seems to appear whenever a big club needs a goal. Named for Alex Ferguson's Manchester United, who scored a lot of late winners.
terms.heard: Sarcastically, by fans of every other club.
terms.sayIt: "Fergie time. Of course they've added six minutes."
terms.overheard: Their lot always get the rub of the green. Fergie time, my dad calls it.
terms.speaker: chat
terms.gist: Stoppage minutes that suit the bigger side
decoys: Kick-off times chosen to suit the television
The seasons a famous manager was in charge

terms.meaning: A small club knocking a big one out of a cup. The FA Cup's whole reputation rests on it.
terms.heard: FA Cup weekends in January and February.
terms.sayIt: "Any giant-killings this weekend?"
terms.overheard: The ground can smell a giant-killing now.
terms.speaker: telly
terms.gist: A small club knocking a big one out of a cup
decoys: A tall side winning everything in the air
A late winner that dumps a team out of a cup

terms.meaning: The FA Cup round in early January, when the Premier League clubs come in. It is the draw that can send a big club to a tiny ground on a wet Sunday.
terms.heard: "Who did we get in the third round?" after the draw.
terms.sayIt: "Third round draw. Who have we got?"
terms.overheard: We've got them in the third round. Of course we have.
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: The FA Cup stage in January the big clubs enter
decoys: The third game of a group in a tournament
The round of matches played on Boxing Day

terms.meaning: The idea that anything can happen in the FA Cup, proved every year by a small club beating a big one.
terms.heard: Commentators, the moment a non-league side scores.
terms.sayIt: "That's the magic of the cup, isn't it?"
terms.overheard: You cannot write this. The magic of the cup, that is.
terms.speaker: telly
terms.gist: The idea that a small club can beat a big one
decoys: A trophy handed over on the pitch at the end
The extra money a cup run brings a club

terms.meaning: A player famous for tough, physical, slightly frightening football. Tackles first, apologises never.
terms.heard: "Proper hard man" about a centre-back or a midfielder who scares people.
terms.sayIt: "He's a proper hard man. You wouldn't want to cross him."
terms.overheard: Signed a proper hard man in the summer. First start today.
terms.speaker: chat
terms.gist: A player feared for his fierce, physical game
decoys: A player who is difficult to deal with off it
A defender who blocks shots with his body

terms.meaning: A player or manager admired for how they behave as much as how they play. Good on the pitch, better off it.
terms.heard: About a player who does charity work or handles a loss with grace.
terms.sayIt: "He's a class act, that one. On and off the pitch."
terms.overheard: What a player he was. Class act, every time I saw him.
terms.speaker: pundit
terms.gist: A man admired for his conduct as much as his play
decoys: A player putting on a show for the cameras
A polished touch that makes the game look easy

terms.meaning: Pundit-speak for very good. Two tops is better than one, and nobody knows why.
terms.heard: Match of the Day, any week.
terms.sayIt: "Top, top player. Genuinely."
terms.overheard: He's a top top player and I don't say that lightly.
terms.speaker: pundit
terms.gist: Pundit-speak for about as good as it gets
decoys: Someone at the top of the scoring charts
A man voted best on the pitch that day

terms.meaning: Someone accused of supporting a club only because it wins. The insult of choice between fans.
terms.heard: Thrown at fans of whoever is winning.
terms.sayIt: "Is he a real fan or a plastic?"
terms.overheard: Listen to them. Plastic fans, the lot of them.
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: A fan who only turns up when things go well
decoys: Someone who turns up in a shop-bought kit
A supporter who watches on TV and nothing else

terms.meaning: A fan who picked a team for its trophies rather than any real connection to it.
terms.heard: "Typical glory hunter" about a mate who supports a club far away.
terms.sayIt: "Why does he support them? Bit of a glory hunter?"
terms.overheard: Glory hunter, him. Always has been, even at school.
terms.speaker: chat
terms.gist: A fan who picked a club for its trophies
decoys: A player chasing his own goals over the team
Someone who collects club shirts and badges

terms.meaning: Liverpool's old coaching room where the next manager was quietly promoted from within. Now means any club that grows its own.
terms.heard: History chats about how Liverpool used to run things.
terms.sayIt: "Is that a boot room appointment, promoted from inside?"
terms.overheard: The boot room was a proper thing once. All gone now.
terms.speaker: pundit
terms.gist: Promoting a manager from inside the club
decoys: The place at a ground where kit is stored
A club's academy for teenage players

terms.meaning: Arsenal's 2003-04 team, who went the whole league season without losing a game. Arsenal fans mention it roughly twice a year.
terms.heard: From every Arsenal fan, about twice a year.
terms.sayIt: "Were the Invincibles as good as everyone says?"
terms.overheard: Their lot will bring up the Invincibles before the first goal.
terms.speaker: chat
terms.gist: A whole league season without a defeat
decoys: A team that went a season without losing at home
A side that won three trophies in one year

terms.meaning: The online corner where fans argue about everything, all day, forever. Not a place for the calm.
terms.heard: "Football Twitter is going mad" about anything at all.
terms.sayIt: "What's Football Twitter saying? Actually, don't tell me."
terms.overheard: Football Twitter has been at it since lunchtime. Not for me.
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: The online corner where fans argue all day
decoys: A club's official account posting the news
The reporters who break transfer stories

terms.meaning: An online game where you pick real players and score points from their real performances. Explains why he cheers for players he hates.
terms.heard: "He's in my fantasy team" about a player he's suddenly cheering for.
terms.sayIt: "Is that a fantasy football thing, or do you actually like him?"
terms.overheard: Don't talk to me about fantasy football this week.
terms.speaker: him
terms.gist: A game where you pick real players for points
decoys: A made-up league played on a games console
Betting on which players will score first

terms.meaning: Old tabloid slang for players' wives and girlfriends, from the 2006 World Cup era. Mostly retired now, thankfully.
terms.heard: In stories about the 2006 World Cup.
terms.sayIt: "Please tell me nobody says WAGs any more."
terms.overheard: My mum still goes on about the WAGs at that 2006 World Cup.
terms.speaker: chat
terms.gist: Tabloid slang for players' wives and girlfriends
decoys: Photographers who chase the players about
The section of the stand kept for families
